nodes.name: Every 6 hours
nodes.notes: Poll, not webhook, because the source is a form export. A webhook would be better and the design does not change: swap this node, everything downstream is untouched.

nodes.name: Fetch applications
nodes.notes: retryOnFail + maxTries + waitBetweenTries is n8n's retry.py. What it does NOT have is jitter: every workflow that failed during an outage retries on the same fixed grid and hits the provider together. At this volume that is fine; at 100x it is the first thing to replace with a Wait node on a random interval.

nodes.name: One item per applicant
nodes.notes: Same reason as steps/ingest.py: one bad applicant must not fail the batch. From here on every node runs per item.

nodes.name: Replayed by 04
nodes.notes: The second entry point. A replay joins here, one item, downstream of the fetch -- so recovering one failed applicant does not re-poll the whole source and re-process the other four hundred. The steps below cannot tell the difference between an item that arrived on the schedule and one that arrived on a replay, and that is the property the whole design is protecting.

nodes.name: Screen
nodes.notes: Calls 00 screening rules. The decision lives in one workflow so that 05 eval can score the same code production runs, instead of a copy that drifts.

nodes.name: Valid?
nodes.notes: A malformed application is data, not an outage. It is dead lettered with reason 'invalid' and never retried, because the payload will be exactly as malformed in five seconds.

parameters.query:
-- Every applicant is stored, including the rejected ones. Keeping only the
-- accepted makes 'how many applied and how many did we turn away'
-- unanswerable, and that is the first question anyone running the programme
-- asks.
INSERT INTO submissions
  (external_id, email, handle, platform, followers, status, reason, raw)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6, $7, $8::jsonb)
ON CONFLICT (external_id) DO UPDATE
  -- Only raw is touched. Two reasons, both load-bearing:
  --
  -- 1. DO NOTHING returns no row, which would break the chain on every
  --    re-poll: the workflow would look like it stopped for no reason.
  -- 2. Updating status would overwrite a human. Somebody moves a 'review'
  --    applicant to 'accepted' in the morning, the poll runs at noon and
  --    silently puts them back. The stored status wins over the computed
  --    one, always.
  SET raw = EXCLUDED.raw
RETURNING id, external_id, email, handle, platform, status,
          raw->>'tracking_code' AS tracking_code;

nodes.name: Store applicant
nodes.notes: queryReplacement is an ARRAY expression, not a comma-separated string. With a string, any value containing a comma (JSON, a reason sentence) shifts every parameter after it by one and the insert either fails or writes the wrong column.

nodes.name: Accepted?
nodes.notes: Reads the status the database returned, not the one the rules computed. That is what makes a human override stick.

parameters.query:
-- Insert-or-fetch, in one statement.
--
-- A plain ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING ... RETURNING returns nothing when the
-- creator already exists, so a replay would stop here instead of going on to
-- retry the email that actually failed. The UNION ALL branch fetches the
-- existing row in that case, and `created` says which happened.
WITH ins AS (
  INSERT INTO creators
    (submission_id, email, handle, platform, tracking_code, rate_cents_per_1k)
  SELECT s.id, s.email, s.handle, s.platform, $2, $3
  FROM submissions s
  WHERE s.external_id = $1 AND s.status = 'accepted'
  ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING
  RETURNING id, email, handle, tracking_code
)
SELECT id, email, handle, tracking_code, true AS created FROM ins
UNION ALL
SELECT c.id, c.email, c.handle, c.tracking_code, false
FROM creators c
WHERE c.tracking_code = $2 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ins);

nodes.name: Create creator
nodes.notes: The WHERE s.status = 'accepted' is a second gate on purpose: this node cannot create a creator out of a rejected applicant even if it is called directly by a replay.

parameters.jsonBody: ={{ JSON.stringify({ to: $json.email, template: 'creator-welcome', handle: $json.handle, tracking_code: $json.tracking_code, idempotency_key: `welcome-${$json.tracking_code}` }) }}

nodes.name: Send welcome email
nodes.notes: Sent AFTER the creator row exists, so a replay re-runs the step cleanly: the insert is a no-op and only the email is retried. Sending first would risk welcoming somebody the database does not have. idempotency_key is derived from the tracking code, so a provider that honours it will not send twice on a retry.

nodes.name: Fetch posts
nodes.notes: The endpoint must echo tracking_code at the top level of the response. That is a contract, not a detail: it is what lets the next node keep the code on every post without depending on n8n's item pairing, which is the part of n8n that breaks quietly.

nodes.name: One item per post
nodes.notes: include: allOtherFields is what carries the echoed tracking_code onto each post.

parameters.query:
-- ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE on (platform, external_id). Without it, polling the
-- same post twenty times would be paid twenty times.
--
-- The SELECT ... FROM creators form means an unknown tracking code inserts
-- zero rows rather than failing: a post for a creator who no longer exists
-- is not an outage. It is also not silent -- the row count is what the run
-- record reports.
INSERT INTO posts
  (creator_id, platform, external_id, url, published_at, views,
   first_seen_at, last_seen_at)
SELECT c.id, c.platform, $2, $3, $4::timestamptz, $5, now(), now()
FROM creators c
WHERE c.tracking_code = $1
ON CONFLICT (platform, external_id) DO UPDATE
  SET views = EXCLUDED.views,
      last_seen_at = EXCLUDED.last_seen_at
RETURNING id, creator_id, external_id, views;

nodes.name: Upsert posts
nodes.notes: views has a CHECK constraint in the schema, so a provider returning a nonsense number fails this insert instead of turning into a nonsense transfer two workflows later.

nodes.name: Waiting for a human
nodes.notes: 'review' and 'rejected' end here on purpose. The applicant sits in the table and the pipeline is done with them. A step that cannot proceed without a decision it is not allowed to make should stop, not guess.

nodes.name: Record run
nodes.notes: One row per execution, appended, never updated. onError continue because observability failing must not fail the work it is observing.

parameters.query:
INSERT INTO dead_letters
  (workflow_id, workflow_name, execution_id, execution_url, node, kind,
   payload, attempts, error, reason)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6, $7::jsonb, $8, $9, $10);

options.queryReplacement: ={{ [$workflow.id, $workflow.name, $execution.id, `${$env.N8N_EDITOR_BASE_URL}/workflow/${$workflow.id}/executions/${$execution.id}`, $prevNode.name, ({ 'Fetch applications': 'ingest', 'Valid?': 'screen', 'Send welcome email': 'onboard', 'Fetch posts': 'track' })[$prevNode.name] || 'unknown', JSON.stringify($json), $json.valid === false ? 1 : 4, $json.reason || $json.error?.message || String($json.error || 'unclassified failure'), $json.valid === false ? 'invalid' : 'exhausted'] }}

nodes.name: Dead letter
nodes.notes: A row, not a log line, so it can be replayed by 04 once the cause is fixed. reason distinguishes 'invalid' (never retry, the payload is wrong) from 'exhausted' (retried four times, the world was wrong).

parameters.jsonBody: ={{ JSON.stringify({ text: `creator-program: ${$input.all().length} item(s) dead lettered in ${$workflow.name} run ${$execution.id}\n${$env.N8N_EDITOR_BASE_URL}/workflow/${$workflow.id}/executions/${$execution.id}` }) }}

nodes.name: Alert once per run
nodes.notes: executeOnce is the whole point: a provider outage fails every item, and thirty failures must not send thirty messages. Alert fatigue is how real failures end up ignored. onError continue so a broken alert channel never fails the run.
